# STAT 110 (synthetic) — Lecture notes

## §1 Conditional probability

§1.1 P(A | B) is read "the probability of A among B". It answers: of the
cases in group B, what share are also in A?

§1.2 Compute it as (number of cases in both A and B) divided by (number of
cases in B). The denominator is the reference group B, not the whole sample.

§1.3 The order matters. P(A | B) and P(B | A) usually differ because they use
different reference groups. Before computing, decide which group the question
restricts you to; that group is the denominator.

§1.4 Assume every case is equally weighted and the reference group is not
empty.

## §2 Two-way tables

§2.1 A two-way table counts cases by two categorical variables at once, one in
the rows and one in the columns, with row totals and column totals.

§2.2 A row percentage divides a cell by its row total; a column percentage
divides a cell by its column total. Choosing row versus column percentages is
the same decision as choosing the reference group in §1.2.

§2.3 Row percentages in one row add to 100%; column percentages in one column
add to 100%. Percentages across a row of column percentages need not.

## §3 Grouped summaries

§3.1 A grouped summary splits the cases by a categorical variable and computes
one summary value (such as a mean or a count) per group.

§3.2 The result has one row per non-empty group, not one row per original case.

§3.3 Compare groups using the same summary; do not compare a group mean with a
group total.

I’m using your study skill and course notes. That opening line is the skill’s study-session marker; we’ll start with explanations and use your answers to guide later practice.

**Conditional probability means finding a probability within a particular group.** Your notes read \(P(A\mid B)\) as “the probability of A among B.” The vertical bar means we restrict attention to group B. [Notes §1.1](materials/notes.md)

For example, suppose a class has 30 students:

- 10 are commuters.
- Of those 10 commuters, 6 have jobs.

Let A mean “has a job” and B mean “is a commuter.” To find \(P(A\mid B)\), ask: **Among commuters, what share have jobs?**

\[
P(A\mid B)
=\frac{\text{number in both A and B}}{\text{number in B}}
=\frac{6}{10}
\]

Report the answer as **60.0% of commuters have jobs**.

The denominator is 10 because the question restricts us to commuters. The other students are outside that reference group. Your notes assume equally weighted cases and a nonempty reference group. [Notes §§1.2–1.4](materials/notes.md)

**Reversing the order changes the question.** Suppose 15 students in the class have jobs. Then \(P(B\mid A)\) asks: among students with jobs, what share commute? The same 6 students belong to both groups, but now we divide by 15: **40.0% of students with jobs are commuters**. [Notes §1.3](materials/notes.md)

A two-way table sorts cases by two categories at once. The key decision is familiar: **which group belongs in the denominator?** Row percentages use the row total; column percentages use the column total. ([Notes §2](materials/notes.md))

For example, consider this new table:

| | Cycles | Does not cycle | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Commuters | 12 | 28 | 40 |
| Noncommuters | 8 | 12 | 20 |
| Total | 20 | 40 | 60 |

“Among commuters, what percentage cycle?” restricts us to the commuter **row**. We calculate \(12/40\): **30.0% of commuters cycle**.

“Among cyclists, what percentage commute?” restricts us to the cycling **column**. We calculate \(12/20\): **60.0% of cyclists are commuters**.

The overlap stays at 12; the reference group changes. Each complete row of row percentages totals 100%, and each complete column of column percentages totals 100%. ([Notes §2.2–2.3](materials/notes.md))

Your turn: **Among people who do not cycle, what percentage are noncommuters?** Give your denominator and answer as a percentage to one decimal place, naming the reference group.
